extracted.intended_audience: MathML authors and implementers (software developers, library authors, spec readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for authoring and encoding mathematical expressions using Content MathML (MathML 3), including when to use non-Strict constructs, qualifiers, binding forms, and how to rewrite to Strict Content MathML. Targeted at implementers and authors producing interoperable semantic MathML markup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid variable capture when using referencing/share
rubrics_metrics.description: Referencing (e.g., share/src references) points to the exact element it references and does not interact with binding intuitively; it allows variable capture to occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using references that capture variables can lead to representation errors and is not recommended. Example: sharing a subexpression g(x) inside a nested lambda can make the shared copy be bound by a different binder (inner vs outer), producing semantic differences after alpha-conversion. Alpha-conversion of the inner binder can break sharing semantics (replacing inner bound x by y changes semantics if share still points to original). Prefer encodings that avoid capture or that use structures where binding is explicit and stable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rendering of share element
rubrics_metrics.description: There are several acceptable renderings for the share element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable renderings include rendering the element as a hypertext link to the referenced element and using the rendering of the element referenced by the src attribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use semantics element for annotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Content elements can be annotated with additional information via the semantics element. MathML uses semantics to wrap the annotated element and the annotation-xml and annotation elements used for representing annotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The semantics element is considered part of both presentation and Content MathML. A semantics element is (strict) Content MathML iff its first child is (strict) Content MathML. See Section 6 'Annotating MathML: semantics' for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of cerror element
rubrics_metrics.description: A content error expression (cerror) is made up of a csymbol followed by a sequence of zero or more MathML expressions; the initial expression must be a csymbol indicating the kind of error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cerror element has no direct mathematical meaning; errors occur as the result of some action on an expression tree and are useful in communication. Errors may occur inside other objects and nested errors are allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enclose only the smallest erroneous sub-expression in cerror
rubrics_metrics.description: Error markup generally should enclose only the smallest erroneous sub-expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A cerror will often be a sub-expression of a larger expression. Example: to encode division-by-zero as part of an equality, put the division-by-zero expression inside a cerror and let the surrounding apply (eq ...) contain that cerror and the other operands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default presentation of cerror
rubrics_metrics.description: Default presentation of cerror is an merror whose first child is a presentation of the error symbol and whose subsequent children are default presentations of the remaining children of the cerror.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one of the remaining children of cerror is a presentation MathML expression, it is used literally in the corresponding merror. Example provided for DivisionByZero showing sample merror presentation ("DivisionByZero: x/0").

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative error context presentation allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: When the context where an error occurs is so nonsensical that its default presentation would not be useful, an application may provide an alternative representation of the error context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: representing an illegal bound variable using a cerror whose child is a cs element containing markup for the illegal construct (e.g., <bvar><plus/></bvar>).

rubrics_metrics.name: cbytes encodes base64 byte streams
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of cbytes represents a stream of bytes as characters in Base64 encoding (matches base64Binary datatype). All white space is ignored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: cbytes is mainly used for OpenMath compatibility and to encapsulate output hard to encode in MathML (binary internal state, image data). Rendering of cbytes is not expected to represent the content; proposed default rendering is an empty mrow. Typically cbytes is used in an annotation-xml or annotated with Presentation MathML.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict Content MathML models mathematical semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: Strict Content MathML encodes logical assertions and expression structure and closely models standard constructions of mathematical logic underlying mathematics; Strict markup can be used to represent all of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict markup is ideal for providing consistent mathematical semantics for all Content MathML expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-Strict idiomatic constructs provided but rewritable to Strict
rubrics_metrics.description: Many idiomatic notational constructs (sums, integrals, sets, piecewise functions, etc.) are not straightforward to represent with Strict Content markup, so non-Strict elements are provided to encode them more directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In all cases, non-Strict expressions may be rewritten using only Strict markup; usually the transformation is completely algorithmic and may be automated. Rewrite rules and examples are provided in section F (The Strict Content MathML Transformation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Container markup vs Strict constructor representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Container markup represents structures by containing markup for constituent elements (e.g., set contains its elements); Strict markup represents set instances as the result of applying a constructor symbol to arguments, where elements are siblings in an enclosing apply element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MathML provides container markup for sets, lists, intervals, vectors, matrices (two elements), piecewise functions (three elements) and lambda functions. There are corresponding constructor symbols in Strict markup for each of these (except lambda which corresponds to binding symbols).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite rules for container markup depend on operator class
rubrics_metrics.description: The rewrite rules for obtaining equivalent Strict Content markup from container markup depend on the operator class of the operator involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To rewrite, consult the operator class and any special case information in the operator syntax table (E) and then apply the rewrite rules described in F (The Strict Content MathML Transformation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Container markup for constructor symbols: explicit vs implicit arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments to container elements that correspond to constructors may be explicitly given as a sequence of child elements, or implicitly given by a rule using qualifiers. Exceptions (interval, piecewise, piece, otherwise) must specify arguments explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example shown: <set>a b c</set> equivalent to apply with csymbol set and children a,b,c. Example with implicit argument: set of even integers using bvar and domainofapplication rewritten to map+lambda in Strict form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lambda container element role and syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: The lambda element is a container element corresponding to the lambda symbol but unlike other constructor containers it performs variable binding; it must have at least one bvar child, optionally followed by qualifier elements, followed by a Content MathML element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The child elements of lambda have distinguished roles. Lambda corresponds to bind in Strict markup; constructor symbols have role application, lambda has role bind. Example of lambda container and equivalent bind form provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of apply to perform variable binding (allowed cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: MathML allows use of apply element to perform variable binding in non-Strict constructions instead of bind in two situations: (1) when the operator to be applied is itself a binding operator (e.g., forall, exists, lambda), and (2) when the operator being applied allows the use of bound variables with qualifiers (e.g., sums, integrals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preserves backwards compatibility with MathML 2 and simplifies encoding of constructs involving bound variables with qualifiers. Example: apply with forall replaced by bind in Strict form; sums/integrals may need lambda introduction in Strict form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alpha-conversion may not preserve meaning for apply-bound variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Because expressions using bound variables with qualifiers are idiomatic and do not always involve true variable binding, one cannot expect systematic renaming (alpha-conversion) of variables bound with apply to preserve meaning in all cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: diff element where the bvar term is technically not bound at all; renaming may change intended semantics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion of apply-binding to bind in Strict form
rubrics_metrics.description: When the operator applied is itself a binding operator, the equivalent Strict representation replaces the apply element with a bind element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: apply(forall, bvar x, apply(geq, x, x)) converts to bind with csymbol 'forall' and the same body. Use bind+csymbol entries for Strict content encoding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite of implicit-binding operators (sums, integrals) to Strict form via lambda
rubrics_metrics.description: When an operator like sum is not itself a binding operator but uses implicit bound variables and qualifiers, the equivalent Strict representation introduces a lambda expression for the summand/integrand and recasts qualifiers as an argument expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: sum with bvar i, lowlimit 0, uplimit 100, body power(x,i) rewrites to apply(csymbol sum, apply(integer_interval 0 100), bind(lambda bvar i, apply(power x i))).

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifier elements: position and order
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualifier elements represent additional idiomatic data (bound variables, limits, domain, conditions); qualifiers always follow the operator and precede any arguments. If more than one qualifier is present, they appear in order: bvar, lowlimit, uplimit, interval, condition, domainofapplication, degree, momentabout, logbase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The precise function of qualifiers depends on the operator/container they modify. Most use cases fall into categories discussed in 4.3; usage notes for specific operators and qualifiers are given in section 4.3.

rubrics_metrics.name: domainofapplication, interval, lowlimit/uplimit, condition semantics and preference
rubrics_metrics.description: domainofapplication, interval, uplimit, lowlimit and condition are primarily used to restrict values of a bound variable. domainofapplication is the most general qualifier and is preferred; interval and lowlimit/uplimit are shorthands that map to domainofapplication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: interval is only interpreted as a qualifier if it immediately follows bvar. condition restricts a bound variable by specifying a Boolean-valued function containing the bound variable and thus requires a preceding bvar. Examples include multiple alternative encodings of a definite integral using domainofapplication, interval, lowlimit/uplimit, or condition. When a bound variable is used the integrand is an expression in the bound variable (not a function).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of condition+domainofapplication for complex domains (multivariate)
rubrics_metrics.description: The general technique of using a condition element together with domainofapplication is powerful and can represent complex/multivariate domains via qualifiers and lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: multivariate integral using two bvar elements, domainofapplication that contains a set with bound variables t,u and a condition combining inequalities; note that the order of inner/outer bound variables is significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: degree qualifier usage
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree element is a qualifier used to specify the degree or order of an operation (roots, moments, derivatives); degree is allowed as the second child of a bvar element for derivatives to indicate order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MathML uses degree for root, moment, and various derivatives. Example: second derivative written as apply(diff, bvar x degree 2, apply(power x 4)). See sections on differentiation and partial differentiation for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized qualifiers momentabout and logbase
rubrics_metrics.description: momentabout and logbase are specialized qualifier elements for use with moment and log operators respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these specialized qualifiers when encoding these specific operators; see operator descriptions for their usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operator classes determine intended usage and rewrite rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Content MathML elements may be broadly separated into classes; the class indicates intended mathematical usage and determines schema usage and applicable rewrite rules for mapping to Strict Content MathML.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operator class of each element is listed in the operator syntax table (E.3). Rewrite rules for mapping to Strict Content are presented in F and include special-case rules and generic rewrite rules (e.g., F.8 Rewrite operators).

rubrics_metrics.name: N-ary operators: explicit vs qualifier-specified arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Many MathML operators may be used with an arbitrary number of arguments either explicitly as children of apply/bind or implicitly via qualifier elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either approach is allowed; however, for n-ary arithmetic operators it's discouraged to use qualifiers and an explicit argument list with plus/times — instead use sum/product when qualifiers represent indexed families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance for n-ary arithmetic operators (plus, times, gcd, lcm)
rubrics_metrics.description: plus and times represent addition and multiplication and accept arbitrary numbers of arguments. They are n-ary commutative operators but using qualifiers with them is discouraged (prefer sum/product). gcd and lcm represent greatest common divisor and least common multiple and may accept explicit arguments or be specified by quantifiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default renderings are locale-specific. Examples show explicit lists of arguments and sample presentation outputs (e.g., x+y+z).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum operator semantics and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: The sum element represents the n-ary addition operator. Terms are normally specified by rule through qualifiers; explicit lists are discouraged in such cases in favor of plus for explicit lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: sum may be used with or without explicit bvar(s). With bvar(s), qualifiers (lowlimit/uplimit/domain/condition) give the domain for index variables and final child is an expression in bound variables. Without bvar(s), final child must be a function evaluated over domain specified by qualifiers. Examples include under/over renderings and alternate encodings using domainofapplication or condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product operator semantics and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: The product element represents the n-ary multiplication operator. Terms of the product are normally specified by qualifiers; explicit argument lists are discouraged (prefer times for explicit arguments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: product may be used with or without explicit bound variables; qualifiers specify index domains (lowlimit/uplimit or condition/domainofapplication). Example renderings and rewrite to Strict supplied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose element semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: The compose element represents function composition. MathML makes no assumptions about domain/codomain of constituent functions; the domain of resulting composition may be empty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: compose is a commutative n-ary operator and may be lifted to collections of arguments indexed by a set using qualifier elements. Examples show nested composition and equality of (f∘g)(x) and f(g(x)).

rubrics_metrics.name: N-ary logical operators (and/or/xor) semantics and qualifier use
rubrics_metrics.description: and, or, xor are n-ary Boolean functions. Arguments may be explicit or specified via qualifiers. and is true iff all arguments are true; or is true if any argument is true; xor is true if an odd number of arguments are true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: and may be used with bvar and limits to express indexed conjunctions; Strict Content equivalents may use apply_to_list/map constructs. Examples show under/over renderings and mapping to csymbols in Strict Content.

rubrics_metrics.name: selector element semantics (indexing into vectors/matrices/lists)
rubrics_metrics.description: The selector element indexes into vectors, matrices and lists. It accepts one or more arguments: first identifies container, subsequent args indicate selection kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With single argument, selector gives the sequence of all elements; for matrices ordering is column then row (a11, a12, a21, a22, ...). With two args and first a vector/list, second arg is index; with matrix and two args, second arg specifies row index. With three args, for a matrix second and third specify row and column; for lists/vectors last arg is ignored. Examples and sample presentations are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: N-ary set operators (union, intersect, cartesianproduct) semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: union denotes n-ary union of sets (contains all elements that occur in any of them); intersect denotes n-ary intersection (common elements); cartesianproduct denotes product of sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These operators take sets as arguments. The specification provides operator syntax and examples for usage and rendering (text ends before full examples in this chunk).
